title: OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol users report missing files, deleted databases: Here’s what we know

reading.body:
OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model deleted files and data in two separate incidents. In one case, a sub-agent misinterpreted a variable during a cleanup task and partially deleted a user's home directory. In another, the model truncated a production database after being asked to clean up test data. OpenAI had documented in the model's system card at launch that Sol takes more unintended actions than its predecessor and cited internal incidents of similar behavior.

The failures resulted from human decisions to bypass or not implement available safeguards rather than from defects in the model itself. One user had enabled Full Access mode based on many prior incident-free sessions, treating the model's restraint as a substitute for actual guardrails. Another user's repository configuration pointed a test database variable directly at production, a configuration problem that no approval system could detect. OpenAI had already published warnings about this behavior at launch, making the incidents foreseeable to users who read the documentation.

It is not established whether these were the only incidents, what proportion of users experienced destructive failures, or what changes OpenAI made in response. Manual backups taken after hearing about the first incident proved to be the only effective protection in both cases, demonstrating a gap between existing safety features and actual safety practice in deployment.

summary:
# Summary

Two prominent engineers experienced destructive incidents with OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol model within one week. Matt Shumer's Mac had its home directory partially deleted when a sub-agent misinterpreted a variable during a cleanup task, while Bruno Lemos's production database was truncated when Sol decided to clean up after generating test data. However, the real story reveals these failures resulted not from model defects but from human decisions to bypass safety features. Shumer had enabled Full Access mode based on hundreds of prior incident-free sessions, treating the model's restraint as a safety mechanism rather than relying on actual guardrails. Lemos's repository configuration pointed his test database variable directly at production, a configuration issue that no approval prompt could detect.

OpenAI had already published warnings about this behavior in Sol's system card at launch, documenting that the model takes more unintended actions than its predecessor and citing internal incidents. The article argues that AI coding safety depends not on smarter models but on users maintaining defensive configurations like separate test environments, credential isolation, and approval tiers for irreversible commands. The real protection in both cases proved to be a manual backup taken after reading about the first incident on social media, highlighting the gap between existing guardrails and actual safety practice.
